newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: INTERVIEW - CRH sees more moderate 97 progress.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - CRH sees more moderate 97 progress.

text.p: CRH Plc said on Tuesday that it sees continued progress in 1997 but does not anticipate the exceptional growth it experienced in 1996.

"We have a bit of digesting to do on some major acquisitions in the United States. We spent about 418 million Irish pounds in acquisitions in 1996," CRH chief executive Don Godson said. "In the nature of things we won't be doing that sort of spend in 1997, it will be more like 150 to 200 million Irish pounds in total."
The group reported an increase of 20 percent in pre-tax profit to 193.43 million Irish pounds in 1996, up from 160.48 million in 1995.

"We have done a lot last year and we have a lot of profits to squeeze out of that," Godson told Reuters in an interview. "We continue to make some progress in Europe and the United States and I think hopefully some downstream additions in Poland and Argentina."

Godson said, longer term, the group hopes to have about 45 percent of its business in the U.S., 45 percent in all of Europe and growing to about 10 percent in emerging economies such as Poland and Argentina.
In 1996, North America accounted for about 42 percent of turnover, mainland Europe generated in the region of 25 percent, Britain and Northern Ireland 19 percent, and Ireland 13 percent.

Godson said there is a lot to be done in the U.S. in terms of integrating deals and finding synergies, particularly with regard to its major acquisition, construction materials group Tilcon, which CRH bought from British conglomerate BTR for $329 million in September 1996.
He said he was very pleased with management's response to the challenges in the U.S.
"There are some painful decisions to be made in cost cutting from disposals but we are pretty well on target so far," Godson said. "We are seeing a good start to the year in the U.S."
Godson said for Ireland the 1997 construction forecast suggests a slowing down from a record 34,000 starts of 1996.
He said the BSE crisis had also affected farmers' incomes and investments "... but I think overall in January and February we have seen a strong start".
He said January was tough in Europe due to inclement weather but it had started to loosen up in February.

Godson said the UK was one of the group's weaker spots in 1996 with profits down about 11 percent but there were some signs of light in the final quarter of the year and sales in 1997 were showing some modest upturn.

"Our businesses there are heavily dependent on housing, to the tune of about 70 percent, but the forecast for 1997 in housing in Britain is about four percent and we are starting to see some signs of that," Godson said. "Our sales are up and there are some modest improvements in markets in January."
Godson said CRH had 12 teams working around the world looking at development prospects.

"They have long shopping lists on things that are very hot and things that are going to take a year or two to bring to the table," Godson said. "So while the search is programmable, the response depends on individual owners and their decisions and whether it is right for them to sell or not."
He said CRH intended to expand broadly within its areas of expertise adding that the group's balance sheet was very healthy and if the right opportunity arose CRH would look at it.
The group declared a debt ratio of 41 percent in 1996 and its interest cover was 8.6 times.
